You have 20 evaluations in total, of which 19 remain. Submit formulations to the evaluator with the evaluate tool, one formulation per call. Each formulation uses at most 9 available ingredients, nonnegative quantities, and no ingredient outside the catalog; fractions are normalized to sum to 1. You can also run Python code with the python tool (numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and pandas are installed; there is no internet access). The working directory contains evaluations.json, which always holds all evaluations so far in the format above; each python call runs in a fresh process, and files you write in the working directory persist. Continue until you have used all evaluations.
I'll systematically explore the formulation space, starting with variations around common chicken analog recipes.

[{'iteration': 1, 'recipe': [{'ingredient': 'soy protein concentrate', 'fraction': 0.32}, {'ingredient': 'soy milk', 'fraction': 0.22}, {'ingredient': 'wheat gluten', 'fraction': 0.18}, {'ingredient': 'pea protein', 'fraction': 0.08}, {'ingredient': 'sunflower oil', 'fraction': 0.06}, {'ingredient': 'potato starch', 'fraction': 0.05}, {'ingredient': 'methylcellulose', 'fraction': 0.03}, {'ingredient': 'yeast extract', 'fraction': 0.03}, {'ingredient': 'flavours', 'fraction': 0.03}], 'target_dissimilarity': 0.335661006037036}]

Let me think strategically. Chicken strips are mainly: water, protein (soy/pea/wheat), small amounts of oil, binders, flavor. The baseline is 0.336. Let me try a few diverse recipes to learn the landscape.
{"iteration": 2, "target_dissimilarity": 0.4843586429015857, "evaluations_remaining": 18}

Oops, I used "salt" which isn't in the catalog. Luckily it looks like it was just ignored. That recipe (no soy milk, more protein) is worse (0.484). So soy milk / water content matters. Let me try something more different.
{"iteration": 3, "target_dissimilarity": 0.4486586452353386, "evaluations_remaining": 17}
More soy milk made it worse too. Original balance is better. Let me try textured vegetable protein which is actually characteristic of chicken strips.
{"iteration": 4, "target_dissimilarity": 0.6332000814767712, "evaluations_remaining": 16}
TVP was much worse. Let me try adjusting composition near the best (iter 1).
{"iteration": 5, "target_dissimilarity": 0.2521985512274595, "evaluations_remaining": 15}
Nice improvement to 0.252! More protein concentrate + wheat gluten helped. Let me push that direction.
{"iteration": 6, "target_dissimilarity": 0.6121680352461023, "evaluations_remaining": 14}
Jumped way worse. The soy milk reduction/wheat gluten increase hurt. So iter 5 was a sweet spot. Let me probe around it.
{"iteration": 7, "target_dissimilarity": 0.3483421507766702, "evaluations_remaining": 13}
Worse than iter 5. Iter 5 is still best. Let me try slight tweaks around iter 5.
{"iteration": 8, "target_dissimilarity": 0.44129811916880846, "evaluations_remaining": 12}
Worse. The small changes matter a lot. Let me try substituting an ingredient to see effect.
{"iteration": 9, "target_dissimilarity": 0.4308641887870209, "evaluations_remaining": 11}

Switching sunflower to canola worsened it (0.252 -> 0.431). Sunflower oil matters. Let me try exact iter 5 but reduce flavours (which may count against us) and redistribute.

Actually iter 5 is very robust. Let me try small, different perturbations.
{"iteration": 10, "target_dissimilarity": 0.6048075437893725, "evaluations_remaining": 10}
Ouch - very sensitive. Let me think. Iter 5 with wheat gluten 0.20, soy conc 0.35 is a sharp minimum. Let me check at 0.36/0.19.
{"iteration": 11, "target_dissimilarity": 0.3235911232126999, "evaluations_remaining": 9}
0.324 - slightly worse than 0.252. The sensitivity is very high. Let me try 0.35/0.20 with slight oil/starch change.
{"iteration": 12, "target_dissimilarity": 0.39189722920863146, "evaluations_remaining": 8}

Worse. Iter 5 (0.252) is still the best. Looking at results, iter 5 seems to be at a local optimum. Let me try changing just one minor ingredient—maybe swap yeast extract for something else, or add a different type.

The landscape is very noisy / sensitive. Iter 5's exact formula is best. Let me try swapping one minor ingredient at a time to see if I can find improvements. Try replacing yeast extract with something more chicken-like.
{"iteration": 13, "target_dissimilarity": 0.3123821670863359, "evaluations_remaining": 7}
Removed yeast extract, moved mass to flavours — worse (0.312 vs 0.252). Let me try adding something distinctive like a flavor ingredient.
{"iteration": 14, "target_dissimilarity": 0.3052909900643056, "evaluations_remaining": 6}
Replacing "flavours" with "plant flavors" was worse too. Let me go back to iter 5 structure but try a different minor swap — replace pea protein with soy protein isolate.
{"iteration": 15, "target_dissimilarity": 0.5177325224499338, "evaluations_remaining": 5}
Worse. Pea protein is better than soy isolate here. Let me try replacing potato starch with another starch.
{"iteration": 16, "target_dissimilarity": 0.3955092612686998, "evaluations_remaining": 4}
Worse. Potato starch is better. Let me try a reasonable alternative - changing methylcellulose amount slightly.
{"iteration": 17, "target_dissimilarity": 0.40840265939090353, "evaluations_remaining": 3}
Worse. Iter 5 remains best at 0.252. Let me try one change swapping yeast extract for a different umami one.
{"iteration": 18, "target_dissimilarity": 0.43046346723174106, "evaluations_remaining": 2}
Worse. Iter 5 formulation is really locked in. Let me try one last variation - maybe add a small amount of 'protein' as a generic to displace flavours.
